claims.text: The initial material is a Co-free equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy in a solid-solution state.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi increases the effective stacking-fault energy.
The altered stacking-fault energy modulates solute–dislocation interaction energies.
Increased stacking-fault energy modifies the energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Removing Co shifts the dynamic-strain-aging regime of equiatomic FeNiCrMn relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
The shifted dynamic-strain-aging regime results from delayed activation of intermittent dislocation pinning and unpinning.
Dislocation pinning and unpinning control the strength–ductility balance at intermediate temperatures and strain rates.
The Co-free alloy will exhibit dynamic strain aging at higher temperatures or lower strain rates than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will have greater early-stage strength associated with the shifted transition.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will have lower ductility at the dynamic-strain-aging transition.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi has a known dynamic-strain-aging regime at intermediate temperatures and strain rates.
The hypothesis is intended to apply from approximately 300 K to 700 K over strain rates spanning multiple orders of magnitude.
The proposed mechanism applies where dislocation-mediated plasticity predominates.
The proposed mechanism does not apply in regimes dominated by diffusion creep or other high-temperature mechanisms.
Processing history and minor compositional variations may affect the stacking-fault-energy change and the dynamic-strain-aging shift.
Indistinguishable dynamic-strain-aging onsets in matched Co-free and Co-containing alloys would falsify the proposed Co-removal mechanism.
